To assess the effect of the IPL treatment of the amorphous SnO 2 on the device properties, we fabricated MAPbI 3 -based planar solar cells using a device architecture of FTO/ESL(I-SnO 2 /ASnO 2 )/MAPbI 3 /spiroMeOTAD/Au, as shown in Fig. 3 (a, b). To optimize the number of IPL pulses for the SnO 2 films, we characterized the PV performance of 20 devices by varying the number of IPL treatment pulses. During each 2 ms pulse, 1.84 J cm -2 of energy was irradiated onto the surface of amorphous-SnO 2 . To optimize the IPL treatment, we varied the number of IPL pulses to as high as 140; the resultant PCEs and the corresponding PV parameters are indicated in Fig. S5.

The perovskite precursor solution (50 wt.%) was prepared by dissolving lead(II) iodide (PbI 2 ; TCI) and methylammonium iodide (MAI; GreatCell Solar) in 0.635 mL of dimethylformamide (DMF; Sigma-Aldrich), to which 70 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; Sigma-Aldrich) was added to form the corresponding adducts [24] . The completely dissolved solution was spin-coated onto an amorphous-SnO 2 ESL layer at 40 0 0 rpm for 25 s, and 0.5 mL of diethyl ether (Sigma-Aldrich) was slowly dripped onto the substrate before the surface became turbid as a result of the rapid vaporization of DMF. The sample was subsequently annealed at 65 ° C for 1 min and then at 100 ° C for 2 min.

evidence.quote: S1 shows a schematic of the IPL setup and the processing parameters corresponding to the various IPL irradiation conditions. Table S1 shows the transferred energy values for each pulse time (1 and 2 ms), as measured by a photosensor (Nova II, Ophir). From ten or more measurements of each transferred energy value, 1.84 J cm -2 of energy per IPL pulse was confirmed to be transferred to the SnO 2 surface under the conditions used to conduct the experiment (60 0 V, 20 0 0 mA, 2 ms, 4 Hz). The SnO 2 films were thereafter subjected to an ultraviolet-ozone (UVO) treatment for as long as 35 min.

Amorphous SnO 2 films were synthesized through a simple solution process using tin(II) chloride dihydrate in ethanol. Hereafter, the amorphous-SnO 2 films that were treated and not treated with IPL are denoted as I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 , respectively. Fig. 1 (a) shows the XRD patterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 , respectively, showing that no crystalline peaks were observed. XPS was used to characterize the chemical bonding states of both amorphous films (A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 ); the resultant spectra are shown in Fig. 1 (b) -(d). Fig. 1 (b) shows the XPS spectra of the Sn 3 d states in A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 .

unresolved_notes: A-SnO 2, I-SnO 2, and heat-treated SnO 2 were retained as processing variants of one family because the finished functional-layer identity remains SnO 2 and the evidence does not establish a different complete architecture or absorber composition for these arms.
The source does not state J-V scan direction; all J-V observations therefore use scan_direction not_reported.
The source does not explicitly establish that the I-SnO 2 device used for EQE was the same physical device as the optimized J-V specimen, so it is represented as a separate individual device.
The source does not explicitly link the hysteresis or EIS specimens to the reported J-V specimens; they are represented as separate measured devices.

The stability comparison reports two unencapsulated devices but does not identify them as any performance devices. It is linked only to the shared family, and no duration or numerical retention value is supplied.

The A-SnO 2 EIS device was measured as part of the comparison, but the reported usable outcomes are phrased as relative properties of the I-SnO 2 device; no separate A-SnO 2 EIS performance observation was invented.

The 20-device IPL optimization reports the number characterized and process-count extrema/optimum, but the supplied evidence contains no complete device-level results for those 20 devices and no extractable numerical distribution from Fig. S5.
Film specimens, electron-only structures, and FTO/ESL/Au structures used for materials, trap-density, conductivity, or mobility characterization were excluded as photovoltaic devices.

The supplied supporting-information pages titled “Intense Pulsed Light Annealing of Tin(IV) Oxide Electron Transport Layer for Largescale Fabrication of Flexible Printed Perovskite Solar Cells” identify a different article and were excluded from this study.

The characterization of 20 devices while varying the IPL pulse count does not itself report an aggregate or distribution. The pulse range and IPL settings are process/optimization conditions, so population-01-ipl-optimization is removed rather than retained as a PopulationStatistic.

The EIS text reports comparative resistance outcomes involving both A-SnO 2- and I-SnO 2-based devices, but its grammar directly attributes the smaller R tr and larger R rec outcomes to the I-SnO 2-based device. No inverse-valued observation was invented for device-07-a-sno2-eis.
